Claude in its current Opus 5.5 form has made some wild reaches in response to reasonable-seeming prompts. For instance: "this error is getting swallowed, make sure the real termination message exposes the root cause" -> discovering that the issue is actually in a third party library that isn't exposing the original error except so through logs, so doing some hackery to inject a log-capturer that gets the stdout, buffers it, and looks for the message in order to re-throw based on that...

And it can demonstrate that working, but it's added some fragile and/or unintended consequences like (a) string matching on a particular WARN log message of a particular version of the lib, and (b) buffering those logs such that there were now cases where they would never make it to the actual output stream before the program terminating.

It's certainly capable of being used smarter than that, but it's also really easy to end up with messy fragile stuff if you get lazy about reviewing the output.

> "this error is getting swallowed, make sure the real termination message exposes the root cause"

Without judgement, I think this illustrates a fundamental objection the anti-AI crowd raises.

The example prompt requires no understanding of what's happening, before suggesting action. Where I work, process requires that a PR review for a solution, has to have a corresponding explanation of why, or it's marked needs work

But a lot of times things in that same vein can be solved sufficiently with a "dumb" prompt like that, so a one-line prompt to get a PR drafted in the background for the dumb stuff can be a pretty good time saver.

The art is not skimping on your attention to the bigger or more important stuff so much that all the time you save on first getting code written is lost by cleaning up stuff like that...

In python, in a co-worker's code, it seems to significantly prefer "some_dict.get('key')" over "some_dict['key']". For the non-python-users, the first one will return None (equivalent to null) when the key is missing, while the second raises a KeyError. It was being used in a whole bunch of places that would cause problems (bad data instead of errors) if it did receive None. Some of these keys were actually optional and it does makes sense for those, but it looks like whichever model he was using just repeated the pattern everywhere instead of just where it was appropriate.

I don't get it... What's the problem? I too prefer getting None as opposed to a key Error which would prolly necessitate a try..catch as opposed just checking for None. I'm having trouble reasoning up a situation where raising a keyError would make any sense over a None for data structures like dicts that could return a value or no value! Help?

KeyError localizes the issue to the lookup (ie “right here this key should be present and it’s not) vs later in the code where it can be hard to trace where the None value came from or how to handle it.
Well... yeah but at the cost of halting your entire program? As opposed to logging?

Think of it like an assert.

Sometimes you do want some flow to terminate if a schema / data contract is breached, and not have this broken data contract propagate elsewhere / outwards.

And/or, it is a perfectly valid pattern to indeed add try..catch, and contain (hence "localize") the issue there and then. If there is a way to handle this breach - you will need some kind of if check anyway. Catching by matching against the particular KeyError exception is in fact robust - and if you forgot to add an intended catch, then the exception will propagate upstack, yes - which is what you want - and this way you do not need to worry about forgetting an "if None" check.

This sort of approach makes it structurally impossible to "forget" - if exception is not caught, it will abort the cannot-be-null breach continuing with program flow, possibly (e.g.) ending up persisted in some place it shouldn't be, causing problems later.
Python uses `except`, not `catch`.

...sure, that's true :) but you get the point.
p.s. and the software design pattern applies in general, imho.
yes, that makes sense. Thank yu so much!

Or you know, test if the key exists before using it. The key could exist and be None, representing a legitimate None at that key. Or the key might not exist and asking for it is a bug.

Use a defaultdict if you must have all keys optional. Using get() everywhere is buggy because it masks illegal key use.

> test if the key exists

Double lookup.

Cheaper than fixing bugs due to illegal key access.

Cheaper than get() masking bugs in your code or dict generation.

But yes let's prematurely optimise for speed in a slow-by-default language by writing bug prone non-idiomatic code. OK.

There are times where you want to check for existence before fetching a key-value pair, and there are times where you want to automatically throw an error if the value doesn't exist.

Both have valid use cases. It's weird to be sarcastic about it.

Oh man, you're giving me flashbacks to a vibe coded utter mess. Gets were a big offender. It seemed to have no discipline to commit to a data format, added all kinds of optional parameters everywhere, was also doing truly insane things like having contingency fallbacks in case some library it wanted to import wasn't where it expected, sometimes even importing things in the middle of a function.

This to me feels more like a developer skills issue than a problem with the LLM. At my day job, we banned using untyped data structures like this entirely well before LLMs because no one could read code that passed them around.

You could use a data structure that better articulates an optional field, like a dataclass with type hints or a pydantic model. Then you, your coworker, and the agent alike, aren’t guessing at whether the key’s value is optional.

Another example in this vein is having many optional parameters on a function or api route, that drive behavior deeply nested in the application logic. Or maybe they were there for testing and never deleted. No one comes across this code next and understands it easily. How could you expect a LLM to understand it, either?

The square bracket version tells the reader it's required, the .get version tells the reader it's optional. Kind of the reason both exist in the language (the .get version has an optional second argument to return instead of None when the key is missing).
The point is that the implementer shouldn’t have to investigate to know whether the key’s value is nullable.
That's when it's accessed, if you just have the data structure you can't tell.

I used Opus 5.5 to figure out that a language model we were serving at work for internal use (we don't really serve models, we only use this internally because it processes sensitive data that we can't send to external endpoints) was being bottlenecked by CPU contention on tokenization, by having Opus run in an autoresearch style loop.

Opus's first proposal for a fix was to spawn multiple Python processes and build a load balancer between them in Python. At first I asked it why it wasn't using haproxy and it said that haproxy would be an added dependency and that the overhead for this kind of thing in Python would be negligible. I knew this was idiotic but wanted to test this out, so had Opus run two experiments in parallel. Sure enough an haproxy load balancer was much, much better on HTTP load balancing than Python code was.

This is the kind of thing that if you're unfamiliar with how networking code works, the models can autopilot into bad decisions that are verifiably correct (higher throughput than the original CPU-bottlenecked implementation) but much short of best practice.

Are you doing CPU inferencing? For small models you could check qxotic.ai which is a whole inferencing stack for many popular open models in Java, which can beat llama.cpp in speed in some cases. Its tokenizer toknroll is faster than tiktoken, which is what made me think of it for your use case.

The advantage is that you don't have issues like the GIL or whatever, so there's no need for all the complexity of load balancing between multiple pythons.

Thought experiment: I'm producing my own synth-pop solo album. I can play guitar, piano, synth, bass, and some saxophone. I need to hire a drummer. I use a black-box service call "Hire-a-Drummer". At no point do I know if the drums were recorded live by a human drummer, if a human hand-programmed the drums, or if the drums were created by AI.

Is there some kind of metaphysical tainting that takes place based on what happens inside of the "Hire-a-Drummer" black-box?

I think so. Regardless of what drummer() is, I think the important part is disclosure, and thus expectations.

If I found out afterwards that your album's songs each had a single long recording of a drum track that you didn't make or refine at all, i'd be upset, because I thought the album was your creative output and that you carefully chose how it was constructed.

If you tell me upfront "the drums are a placeholder while I work on how to do them" then I can still enjoy the rest of the album, whether that part of the track is AI or not. But if you instead were to go in and take the time to carefully craft the drum track for the album, I don't care if AI was used to make the actual waveforms of the drum beats.

I think the problem is that, the more AI is used as a way to take shortcuts in your work, the less I can attribute to you, and the more it's just "correct" and thus generic. If you use AI as a tool to enable you to do creative work, then I think it's fine, I just want to know what I should judge as being 'you'.

Similar thing: Epic: The Musical is a concept album made in Logic Pro X. None of the instruments actually played or were recorded (at least by Jorge). But I enjoy the album on the basis of how Jorge's mind arranged the instruments, how the songs are written, the humans singing it and the emotions they put into their performance, etc. I don't think anyone thinks Jorge hired an orchestra nor sat there and played all those instruments himself.

So, when someone says that they like the trumpet in some part of a song in Epic, they're actually saying that they enjoy (A) the trumpet is there at that specific moment, and (B) and what decisions Jorge made for it - like its length, any effects added to create its sound profile, etc. This person probably subconsciously knows that Jorge did not actually blow into a trumpet to make that part of the song.

I think code coverage like many things is a “it depends”.

I think 100% code coverage usually means that for every branch, there is some test that results in it going down that branch? Like, there’s no line of code (outside of potential exception handling code?) that isn’t “tested” by any test (where “tested” means “it gets run during the test”).

>> If I have a function add_nums that takes 2 numbers and adds them, there are like infinite inputs that can be tested.

That's what formal verification is for: you generate math statements from the code, and then prove them.

Testing is for covering the most common scenarios and likely edge cases. 100% coverage means every line of code in the app is executed when your test suite runs. It is useful as a bare minimum, but by itself does not guarantee that there are no bugs.

Hardware companies (and Japanese hardware companies in particular) don't care for or understand the rules that govern software.

Neither do governments, incidentally. They're okay-ish at skyscrapers and bridges, but software is just beyond them.
Any take on why that is the case?

I'd say that hardware manufacturers are not accustomed to software flexibility.

They may treat changing a timeout value like changing a capacitor with one of a different value on a PCB. Doing it is slow and expensive, involving suppliers, delays, testing campaigns, etc... So that's the kind of thing that is specified up front, to avoid having to touch anything in production. If a change is needed, it will go in V2, months later at best.

It has some advantages, such as not breaking things that work, but they are also not fixing things that don't.

To add on I've seen a lot of instances where hardware people build software...like hardware people. They think in terms of relays and maybe PLCs and build their software along that model. They're sort of stuck thinking in terms of hundreds or thousands of Hertz. They don't really internalize that a little silicon bit can run at hundreds of megahertz and read sensors thousands or millions of times per second.

It's not about being dumb, I think it comes from the mental model where big electrical appliances/machines are controlled by big slow relays and switches. Changes to the state of operation involve inertia and momentum and huge power spikes and fuses that make extremely loud noises when they blow.

Doesn't need to be open source in itself, we need standards that are used and shared.

Even if its closed on their end, having standards is the key.

Standards that require a new vocabulary of already overloaded words and concepts are not that good. Often you can't know part of a standard and be better off for it. If you want wide adoption, don't target the narrow.

A good standard lets the bad users grow into better users. It's like the gap between novice vs pro graphics software. It's a novice trap. I like to think of the evolution of Factorio. It's been 15 years with the same core team playing their own game in a LAN party every week, as well as individually. And it's high quality.

Dogfooding led them to counter-intuitive decisions like, if a flying robot runs out of battery, it should obviously crash into the ground and explode, but it turned out way better for gameplay if it just limps slowly to the nearest charging point instead. This fact and many more can only be discerned from actual gameplay experience. No amount of pure linguistic reasoning will tell you them. Another one is how the burner inserters (coal-powered robot arms) fuel themselves - in the first version, they didn't. They could have made running around to refuel your robot arms a part of the game, but that isn't where they discovered the statue within the marble. You had to try the game both ways and see what feels more fun. A third: filter inserters and smart inserters were removed, and their features were moved to all inserters. A fifth: basic oil processing used to produce all three oil products, and now it doesn't. A sixth: the basic oil refinery has its liquid I/O ports set up in a way that's compatible with switching to advanced oil refining later, instead of requiring you to redo your pipes.

I have yet to see LLMs do well “autonomously” on anything that doesn’t fall into any of these 3 buckets:

1. well specified

2. well tested (which is a form of spec)

3. represented in the training set (i.e. not built on a corpus of human developed examples)

For example, a lot of the compiler porting efforts fall into all 3 buckets: compilers are well specified (there is a set of valid inputs and an expected behavior), they are typically well tested, and as a bonus, in a way that is implementation agnostic thanks to the clean interface (think: integration vs unit tests), and are very well represented in the training set.

You can "solve" 1 and 2 by N-version programming. Have the same code implemented twice, or more times, you get free error testing by fuzzing or running replicas in shadow mode. In order to make replicas maximally different choose a different language, framework, agent harness and LLM.

There remain some nitty details related to tracking randomness and choosing what interfaces to log. But even having your code testable by replicas would help organize it better and expose different assumptions made by the language or library stack.

When you get different outputs from replicas it can be 1. one of them has a bug, or 2. the spec is unclear -> fix the bug or the spec. So this method catches both sides. It also might be faster than traditional code based testing, you can build replicas in parallel. A replica is an open ended test, unlike coded tests it can be tried on open ended input values.

The core idea is that it is easier to implement twice than to imagine bugs. We already solved implementation, but bug finding means running code in your head, it touches the halting problem issues - can we really imagine behavior from code? I don't think we can do it well. Ambition has to match the problem space. Sometimes I stare at the Bay Bridge here in San Francisco, and I wonder to myself, as an exercise of "how much more ambitious could AI make us?" imagining a 10x version.. would it simply be a bridge 10x bigger? Is that the best I could come up with though? And why is the bridge there at all? ~15,000 years ago you could have walked from SF to Oakland across a dry valley floor (that is now the Bay, true story). Then the glaciers melted, water flooded in, and only then did crossing it become a problem worth solving: first with boats, then with a bridge, and eventually with BART’s Transbay Tube, which isn’t a bigger bridge at all.

Bridges exist to move people and goods across water within a particular envelope of needs and constraints. In this specific case, when the needs grew, the most ambitious answer was not a bigger bridge, but BART's Transbay Tube, which is an entirely different kind of thing.

So when I reflect on Dan's piece, it seems we're in agreement that AI is not provoking us to simply build bigger versions of things we already have.. but what remains unsettled is whether we know what we’re really building for yet.

There's of course the by-now oft-repeated story of electrification of factories, which had a 'first pass' of mostly swapping out the steam engine with one big motor, and otherwise preserving the same layout. Over time people redesigned floor plans around small motors at each machine (with Paul David’s “The Dynamo and the Computer” being the classic telling of this).

A lot of AI-assisted software development right now still feels like the one-big-motor pass at this. I suspect the projects really worth being ambitious about are probably the ones that only make sense once the entire factory floor changes, and I don’t think we're able to see that just yet. What Dan's doing is probably the right answer at the moment, building a lot of odds things and seeing what sticks.

Back to the Bay story, I think this moment is equivalent to our digital glaciers melting, and the water rushing in, than us having to figure out better "cranes", for example. It's changing what the world we're designing for is, what the whole problem space is, instead of whether we build bigger versions of things within the prior paradigm.

We look to our software stack today and we are tempted to imagine 'bigger', 'better', 'faster', 'more efficient', but... why? What are we really building _for_? We shall see!
